div.head: Disputation 2
De objecto, seu subjecto materiali fidei
div.p:
DISPUTATIO II.
DE OBJECTO, SEU SUBJECTO MATERIALI FIDEI.

Three things distinguished in the object of faith. — I do not treat the question that is usually premised in any science concerning its subject matter, whether it exists; for I presuppose that faith exists, from what was said in the treatise on grace, and from what will be said below on the necessity of faith and on its habit; especially since, from the testimonies of Sacred Scripture adduced in the preceding disputation, it is sufficiently evident that there is in us an intellectual, supernatural, and infused faith. Having set aside, therefore, the question whether faith exists, we begin to investigate what it is; and so we take our beginning from the object, because the whole virtue is ordered to it. Now in this object St. Thomas, in the Secunda Secundae, question one, article one, distinguishes three things: namely, the material object — that is, the subject matter with which the virtue is concerned — and the formal object — that is, the aspect under which it is concerned, or the motive on account of which faith believes. The third Thomas calls accidental, and in the replies to the arguments explains that under this heading he includes all created objects, which he says pertain to faith secondarily and, as it were, consequently. I, however, include all those things that are believed on the basis of divine testimony under the material object of faith, as I will explain in the second section; and so I understand that third member differently: for beyond the material and formal object, there is required for believing a sufficient proposition of the doctrine of faith, according to that text: How shall they hear without a preacher? For since neither God testifying nor the things testified to are seen, it is necessary that they be sufficiently proposed through hearing — for faith is therefore said to be from hearing. These three things, therefore, are to be explained by us in the same order, and we begin with the material object, as the clearer. In this, furthermore, subject (subjectum) can be distinguished from object (objectum); for, although these terms are more frequently confused and we use them interchangeably in a good sense, now, for the sake of clarity, we distinguish them, following Durandus in Book One, Question Five of the Prologue, and in Book Three, Distinction Twenty-Four, Question One; and Capreolus, Question Four of the Prologue, Article Two. We call the subject (subjectum) the simple or incomplex thing about which something is believed, because it is the subject of that proposition which is believed; but the complex and believed proposition itself is called the object (objectum), because it is that which faith
immediately believes and to which it assents; each of these, therefore, is to be explained separately.

div.head: Sectio 1
An deus sub ratione deitatis sit subjectum principale fidei
div.p:
SECTIO I.
An Deus sub ratione Deitatis sit subjectum
principale fidei?

1. First assertion concerning faith. — Setting aside opinions that will be touched upon incidentally later, since they are not of great moment, the first thing to be said is that God is the subject (subjectum) of Christian faith. This is self-evident and certain in faith, because our faith tends toward God and is concerned with God, and is therefore one of the theological virtues, 1 Corinthians, chapter thirteen; and so, in Mark eleven, Christ says: Have faith in God; and Paul, in 1 Thessalonians 1: faith which is toward God, etc. Hence Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 5 for the Illuminated: Faith, he says, contemplates God, gazes upon God. The reason indeed is that we believe many things about God — namely, that he exists, and that he is one and triune, etc. Therefore God is the subject of faith, according to the explanation already given.

9. Second assertion, most certain. — Second, it must be said that God is the principal subject (subjectum) of faith, which is customarily called the subject of attribution of a virtue or habit; the theologians to be cited shortly agree on this as well, and it is nearly equally certain. First, from the manner of speaking of Scripture: Hebrews 11: Without faith it is impossible to please God; and it immediately adds: For one who draws near to God must believe that he exists; it therefore sets forth God as the primary term toward which faith tends. And so Ephesians four says: One Lord, one faith; and Colossians two: unto the knowledge of the mystery of God, signifying that all faith tends principally toward knowing God — which is also found in Colossians three and Philippians one. And so Christ says in John 14: You believe in God; believe also in me, because that is primary and this is consequent. Hence Augustine, City of God, Book 4, Chapter 20, says: The first and greatest office of faith is that the one God be believed; and in Book 11, Chapter 2, he says that the end of all faith and of Christ himself is to arrive at God. And this is the reason for the assertion: the principal subject of attribution is that to which all things are referred that fall under a virtue or habit; but all things revealed through faith tend toward God being better known and honored;
therefore. Likewise, in the blessed life God is the primary object; therefore also in faith, because the vision of faith succeeds it. Hence in John 17, Christ says: This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, which the Fathers understand of both the homeland and the way. Finally, the light of faith is a certain supernatural participation in the divine light; but God himself is the primary object of the divine light by essence, and of the created light of glory; therefore also of the light of faith. It can be asked, however, whether this is from the intrinsic nature of such a quality or from divine ordination; but this will be better explained a little below.

3. Durandus holds the view contrary to the preceding assertion. — His foundation is refuted in two ways. — Against this assertion, however, Durandus, Question 5 of the Prologue, held that the meritorious act is the principal object of Theology; he had explained that by Theology he means faith. His argument is that all things handed down in Scripture are ordered toward the merit of glory to be obtained in this life. But this is an improbable opinion, in which he himself did not persist, for in Book Three, Distinction 24, Question 1, number 7, he teaches our conclusion. And his argument is of no force, and proves the contrary, because merit itself is ordered toward glory, and created glory toward God himself. There is also another reason to avoid this opinion of Durandus: namely, because it has a certain affinity with the opinion of Chemnitz and the heretics of this time, who say that the principal object of faith is God's promise concerning our justification and the remission of sins through Christ. These err most gravely when they speak of this promise as absolute and made to each individual believer in particular — which is false and heretical, as the Council of Trent teaches, and as I have discussed at length in the treatise On Grace, Book 8, from Chapter 15. Nevertheless, even if one speaks of the general promise made under the due condition — which indeed is one of the things to be believed — it still cannot be called the primary material subject; for this promise itself is ordered toward God, and so pertains to the secondary objects of belief.

4. An Objection Against the Same Assertion from the Council of Trent. — Response. — Certain words of the Council of Trent can be raised as an objection, Session 6, Chapter 6, where, explaining what is necessary to believe for justification, it says: and first of all, that God through his grace remits sins on account of Christ; therefore it posits this as the primary subject of justifying faith. The response, however, is easy: the Council first premised those words: they are disposed toward justification when, aroused by divine grace and conceiving faith from hearing, they freely move toward God, believing those things which have been revealed; the first movement, then, it places in God as the primary object; but in the other subordinate words it declares how that faith is to be applied to conceiving penitence with due trust, for which the consideration of God through faith as remitting sins is especially helpful, in which it is also not excluded that God himself is the primary object around which that faith is concerned, but only through it something secondary is believed about God, such as his being a justifier, which will be more fully explained in the following assertion.

6. Against This Assertion: the Views of Gregory of Rimini, Thomas of Strasbourg, and Others. — Calvin's Objection. — Both Are Refuted. — Against this assertion, however, many theologians have held that God, under the ratio of Savior or Glorifier, is the subject of faith, which is the view of Gregory of Rimini, Prologue, question 4, and Thomas of Strasbourg and Giles of Rome, and others there, speaking about the subject of Theology, as is treated more extensively in the beginning of Part 1. Their foundation is that all things revealed through faith are ordered to the salvation and glory of human beings, according to that passage, John 20: these things are written so that you may believe, and believing may have life in his name. Hence also Calvin rebukes the Scholastics on the grounds that they say God, as God, is the primary subject of faith, and not also God as man, that is, Christ, since faith in Christ is demanded above all in the Gospel and our salvation is attributed to him. But these opinions have no solid foundation. For we must distinguish two orders of predicates or perfections that are known of God: some are altogether necessary and intrinsic to God, such as being one, triune, and good; others are contingent, or free, and in some way extrinsic to God, such as being actually creator, justifier, and so forth. Although faith therefore knows God as the subject to which all these belong, since it believes all these things about him, it is nonetheless certain that predicates of the first order are prior and primarily intended by faith; for all other things are ordered to the manifestation of those attributes of God: God creates so that he may be known as omnipotent, and so with the rest. Therefore God cannot be the subject of faith under any extrinsic or contingent ratio or denomination, such as those of Savior or Glorifier, and so forth. Nor does it matter that faith is ordered to our salvation and glory, because our very salvation and glory is itself ordered to the glory of God and the manifestation of his nature; just as charity too is ordered to our salvation, and yet its object is God according to himself and according to the absolute goodness he has in himself; and this is generally true of each theological virtue according to its own ratio. Now Calvin's objection is either empty or false: for if he says that theologians omit Christ altogether in assigning the material object of faith, he says something utterly false, as will be clear from what follows; but if he objects because they place him not in the first position but in the second, he speaks against Christ himself, who says, believe in God, and believe also in me; and elsewhere: this is eternal life, that they know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent; and the same order is observed in the creeds of faith, for first are taught the things that pertain to divinity, then those that pertain to humanity; and so rightly says St. Thomas, Summa II-II, q. 176, art. 6, that faith consists principally in two things: first in the knowledge of God, and then in faith in the Incarnation.

7. A Doubt from the Text of St. Thomas. — Resolution. — Satisfaction of St. Thomas's Text. — Someone may ask, since there are many divine attributes that necessarily belong to God, whether God is subject to faith according to some determinate attribute, or according to the whole collection of them. And the reason for doubt can be that St. Thomas here, in article one, said that God under the aspect of first truth is the formal object of faith, and he seems to speak not only of the formal ratio under which, but also of the ratio which is primarily known; yet to be first truth is a particular attribute of God. I respond that God is not the primary object of faith according to some special attribute conceived by us in the manner of a property or some power of God, but according to the absolute aspect of Deity, in which, in a confused or quasi-radical way according to our manner of conceiving, all attributes are included. This is gathered from the cited authors and the scriptural testimonies adduced; and the reason is that faith primarily intends the knowledge of the true God by essence; but the essence of God essentially includes all attributes, and therefore faith of itself does not first tend toward any special attribute, but toward Deity as such. But if, according to our manner of conceiving, the substance of God is understood under the absolute concept of essence, and the other attributes as consequent properties according to reason, then God, according to the aspect of his essence, is the primary object, in accord with the text: he who comes to God must believe that he exists; for, as I have said, the very being of God is conceived as the primary essence of God, because he is being itself by essence,
in accord with the text: I am who I am. Nor does the above-cited statement of St. Thomas conflict with this; for a twofold truth in God must be distinguished, namely truth in being and truth in speaking, concerning which distinction more will be said in the following chapter. The former truth is not properly a special attribute of God, but is transcendental truth, which adds nothing to the nature of a thing, and so true Deity says nothing other than Deity itself; and it is this truth that is meant when it is said that God, as first truth, is the primary material object of faith — which amounts to saying that God, according to his true Deity, and thus according to his essence, is such an object. The latter truth, however, is a special attribute, and belongs primarily to the formal object, as we will say below; but insofar as it is also the thing believed, it is not properly the primary object according to aspect, but comes after Deity as such, although perhaps, with respect to the other attributes, it has a certain priority according to aspect, as I will touch on presently and treat more fully in the following disputation.

8. The Fourth Assertion Proceeding in a Twofold Sense. — The Difference between Human and Divine Faith. — Fourth, it must be said that among the material objects of faith, God is the most necessary and inseparable from the revelation of faith. This can be understood in two ways. In one way, concerning the necessity relative to the end of the one revealing, and to the worship and honor due to him, and also to the salvation of those to whom the revelation is made; and in this sense the matter is clear, because unless God were to speak to human beings about himself, he could not be worthily worshipped by them, in accord with Romans 10: How will they call upon one in whom they have not believed? Nor could they be saved, since the salvation of the human person is placed in God, and without faith in God a human being cannot please God, Hebrews 11. In another way the assertion can be understood of the intrinsic and essential necessity of the habit of faith itself, and it is in this sense too that I understand the conclusion. The reason is that nothing is believable through faith except under divine testimony, as I now presuppose; therefore whoever believes something through infused faith believes that it has been revealed by God and that the testimony of God is infallible; therefore it is impossible to believe anything by divine faith that is not God, without something being presupposed as believed about God himself — which must be, at minimum, that God exists and is truthful in what he testifies. Thus God, as material object, or as the thing known, has a necessary connection with faith that the other objects do not have; for God could reveal many things about himself and nothing about creatures.
And here must be noted a difference between human and divine faith; for through the faith by which we believe some human being, we need not believe anything about the speaker himself; for his existence and his speaking we do not believe but see; and as for his being truthful, or worthy of belief, even if we perhaps do not see this, we nonetheless do not believe it on his testimony but presuppose it as known from elsewhere, at least through conjecture. In divine faith, however, it is not so, because God cannot through this faith reveal anything to us without in some way revealing himself, since we do not see him speaking or existing but believe it, nor do we believe him to be truthful through other conjectures or reasons alone, but through the same faith which tells us: God, however, is truthful. You will say: granted this is true for wayfarers, yet among the blessed who see God, it could happen that God testifies to them something outside himself and not yet seen by the blessed, even in the Word, and so a revelation of faith could be given concerning a created thing and not concerning God, since he is already seen; and thus seems to have thought Scotus, in Book 3, d. 30. But this touches on the question of whether faith can exist in the blessed, which I will treat below; for now I say briefly that that revelation, if it is in some way founded on the vision of God speaking, does not belong to infused faith but is a knowledge and light of another kind, and therefore presents no obstacle to the conclusion stated.

div.head: Sectio 2
Utrum deus sit adaequatum subjectum materiale fidei, vel quod illud sit
div.p: SECTION II. Whether God is the adequate material subject of faith, or what that subject is.

3. First Objection. — Reply. — You will say: faith cannot extend to everything revealable; therefore that is not the adequate object, since such an object is coextensive with the habit.
The antecedent is clear, because faith can believe only what has been revealed; but there are many revealable things that have not been revealed; and also because revealable things are infinite, yet faith cannot extend to infinitely many things. The response is that speaking of aptitude is one thing, speaking of act is another. It is true that faith cannot elicit or exercise an act except concerning things that have been revealed; yet the very light of faith is of itself apt to assent to whatever is revealable, if it were in fact revealed; and in this sense we say that being revealable is the adequate object, and we speak rather of the revealable than of the revealed, so that we may not appear to exclude altogether what has not been revealed, and so that we may better explain the nature and power of faith. And in the same way it must be said that, although faith in act always extends to finite things, it can of itself extend to infinitely many things syncategorematically, as they say, because this does not exceed the power of a finite faculty or habit, as Scotus above rightly shows, and St. Thomas, the said art. 8 of De Veritate, ad ultimum.

4. Second Objection. — Reply to the Objection. — A further objection can be raised: not all things revealed through faith are equally believable; therefore not all are directly contained under the adequate material object of faith. The antecedent is clear because not all things are equally true, for divine things are more true than created things, since they are more necessary and more beings. This is confirmed first because with respect to charity, God and creature are not equally comprehended under its object; therefore neither with respect to faith. Finally, St. Thomas above says that all things outside God belong to faith only per accidens; therefore this is a sign that they do not belong to its direct object, just as what is only accidentally visible is not the direct object of sight. To the argument the response is by denying the assumption. Indeed, the assertion is thereby confirmed, because truths of faith about a created subject are no less certain than those about an uncreated subject; for this proposition is just as certain: the most Blessed Virgin is the Mother of God, as this one: God is three and one; because each equally participates in the formal aspect of faith, which is to be said by God, and God is equally truthful and infallible in small matters as in great ones, for he would forfeit all his truthfulness and authority if he could say something false in even the smallest matter; and therefore no less is a heretic, and loses the whole faith, one who denies one of those truths
than one who denies another. The antecedent is therefore false; and its proof suffers from an equivocation, for it is one thing to speak of the truth of a thing in itself and its knowledge through intrinsic principles, and another to speak of truth in the being of the credible, which is founded on extrinsic testimony. In the former truth there is inequality between the created and uncreated object; but this is irrelevant to faith as such; what matters is credibility, which arises from testimony, and this is equal in things that are in themselves unequal, because the testimony is the same and equally informs the thing testified, as I would say. And from this the response to the first confirmation is clear: for in charity the divine goodness is participated in extrinsically by the creature, and therefore it is not equally present in the creature and in God, and for this reason creature and God are not equally loved through charity; but revelation, or the testimony of God, extrinsically informs credible things, and therefore can fall equally on created and uncreated objects — a doctrine drawn from St. Thomas, Book 3, dist. 29, q. 1, art. 2, ad 1. To the second confirmation the response is that St. Thomas used the phrase per accidens broadly, to signify the same as through another, or by reason of another, or secondarily; but when speaking in terms of the credible object, a created subject is believed per se just as much as an uncreated one, if something has been revealed about it in itself and properly.

5. The Third Assertion, in Two Parts. — I say third: God can in some way be called the adequate direct or indirect object of faith, or partly in the direct sense and partly in the oblique sense. The first part is self-evident: for God is believed through faith, indeed most of all and principally, as is clear from the preceding section. The second part is drawn from St. Thomas here, art. 1, where he compares faith to the science of medicine, which, having health as its object, treats other things insofar as they lead to health: thus, he says, faith believes either God or what pertains to God; the same point is made in the said art. 8 of De Veritate, in the replies to the arguments; and St. Thomas, Part 1, q. 1, art. 7, on the object of Theology holds the same, concerning which we said the argument is the same; and in the same sense theologians commonly, both in the Prologue of the Sentences and in Book 3, dist. 23 and 24, teach that God is the object of attribution of faith or theology — that object of attribution being called what all things that fall under the habit are referred to. From this is drawn the argument for the assertion: because all things believed through faith are ordered to God,
as was also said in the preceding section; therefore all things are believed as in some way divine, or pertaining to God; therefore in every object about which faith believes something, God is in some way included; thus God is the adequate object of faith, directly or obliquely — which can also be confirmed by induction: for in the mysteries of divinity the matter is clear; and the mysteries of the Incarnation all have to do with God; and angels and human beings are made in God's image and are his temple, they flow from him and tend toward him, and it is under these titles that they fall under faith; and the same holds for the rest.

6. A Doubt. — Resolved. — You will say: sins are neither contained in God, since they are not his works, nor are they referred to God, as is clear; and yet they pertain to the material subject of faith, for many things about sins are believed through faith; therefore with respect to those things God cannot be called the adequate object of faith, even obliquely. I respond that just as sins fall under divine knowledge, so they can be contained under the object of faith; for divine knowledge has its own essence as its adequate object in some way, and yet through it God knows sins as contrary to his goodness, and thus God is said to know evil through the good. In the same way, then, faith reveals sins insofar as they are turnings away from God, and so even with respect to them God is the object in some respect — not because God is the end toward which sins are ordered, but because he is the end from which they turn away, and consequently because they are judged by God and ordered to punishment, through which divine justice is manifested.

7. A Minor Question Arising. — The Response and Argument of Some. — The True Response. — But someone will ask whether this mode of relation to God is so essential to faith that it is inseparable from it, such that it is impossible for something to be believed by the true assent of infused faith without being ordered to God, both as believed through faith and as supernatural end. Some think so, and the argument can be that faith is essentially an infused virtue, and therefore by its nature and from within is ordered to the supernatural end; therefore it is essential to it that all things believed through it be ordered to the same end; therefore, by reason of this relation, it is essential to this virtue to have God as its adequate object in the stated sense. Also because this seems essential to a theological virtue as such, as can be shown from other cases; but faith is a theological virtue; therefore. Nevertheless I respond that this is not essential to faith according to the actual ordering of all credible things to that supernatural end, but that an aptitudinal order suffices —
namely the innate relation that every creature has to God. This is briefly explained and proved: for God could have ordered the human being to a natural end, as has been shown in the treatise on Grace, and nevertheless something could be revealed to that person to be believed through faith — for example, the creation of the world or the immortality of the soul; therefore in that case those created things would be subjects of faith without an actual relation to that supernatural end, retaining only the aptitudinal one. What some say — that in that case the faith would not have been supernatural — does not seem probable to me, because it would have the same formal aspect of believing and consequently the same certitude, which cannot be had without the help of infused faith. Hence the a priori argument is that the essence of a virtue is taken from its motive or formal object, and therefore on the side of matter it is only essentially required that the matter be sufficiently contained under the formal objective aspect; but the order of one partial matter to another is not so essential, except insofar as it conduces to or is necessary for participation in the formal object. To the argument on the other side the response is that for an infused virtue and its supernatural act, it suffices that the aspect under which the virtue tends be supernatural. And for the nature of a theological virtue, it would suffice that the principal object immediately attained through it be God — and this faith has by its own nature. Hence it can also be said that it is connatural to faith that all credible things through it be ordered to God, as St. Thomas held, the said q. 14 of De Veritate, art. 8, ad 18, and as the argument made above suggests; yet it cannot be called essential according to actual ordering, since this depends on the free will of God.

div.head: Sectio 3
An objectum quod immediate creditur per fidem complexum sit, et quotuplex
div.p: SECTION III. Whether the object immediately believed through faith is complex, and in how many ways.

2. Second Assertion. — The Heretics' Threefold Division of Faith. — Refuted from Scripture. — Second, it must be said that the various complex truths of faith, while many, are all composed into one single object of one faith, because they all agree in the same credible thing. This assertion is put forward partly to explain the complexity of this object, partly because of the heretics of this age; for they distinguish three faiths, which they call historical, of miracles, and of promises; and they subdivide this third into two, namely into a general faith, which concerns universal promises, such as: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; and a special faith, by which each just person, in order to be such, must formally believe that his sins have been forgiven him and that he will infallibly attain glory — and this last they call justifying faith. But beyond this last error concerning this special faith, which was refuted in the treatise on Grace, book 8, chapter 16, they err further by multiplying faiths, since Paul says in Ephesians 4: One Lord, one faith;
and in 2 Corinthians 4: Having the same spirit of faith; hence in Hebrews 11, to this same faith, which he had said was the evidence of things not seen, he attributes all those gifts; for when he says: By faith we understand that the ages were fashioned by the word of God, he posits historical faith; but when he says that Abraham and Sarah through faith had a son, he clearly posits faith of promise, saying: Because she judged faithful him who had promised; and what he adds about the sons of Israel: By faith they crossed the Red Sea, pertains to faith of miracles; and further below he encompasses all, saying: By faith they conquered kingdoms, they worked justice, they attained the promises; although therefore it is true that the matter of faith encompasses those three things, nonetheless there is the same faith concerning all of them, and among them there is only a material diversity.

3. From Reason. — Furthermore, it must be added that this very material (so to speak) multiplication of the objects of faith is not rightly or sufficiently explained in that way; for that God exists, and is triune, and similar dogmas, pertain neither to history, nor to promises, nor to miracles. But if they wish to comprehend these under history, then faith of promises also pertains to history; for the fact that God promised this or that is a kind of history, which faith believes; but the fact that he will fulfill what he promised pertains to the dogma of faith, by which we believe God to be truthful and faithful. And nearly the same holds for faith of miracles, insofar as it is catholic, because through it we believe both that God can work a miracle, since we believe him to be omnipotent, and that he will do so as he promised, if the necessary conditions concur. There is therefore no need to use these distinctions, but there is one faith embracing many dogmas, as we said in the assertion, under which it is true that histories and promises are comprehended, and moreover the truths by which the nature of God is revealed to us.

4. Third Assertion. — Resolution of an Objection. — It must further be added that the object of faith embraces not only necessary truths, such as that God exists and the like, but also contingent ones, whether of the past or of the future, such as: the Antichrist will come, or: there will be a universal judgment; this is established from the divine Scriptures, and the reason is that all these things are revealed. You will say: faith must be certain; but certainty can only concern necessary things.
The reply is that, just as the knowledge of God is certain even though it concerns contingent things — because it attains them according to the state of presence and necessity, by which everything that is, necessarily is — so faith concerning contingent things can be certain, because it attains them as they stand under divine revelation, which flows from the knowledge of God.

5. Fourth Assertion. — Finally, this object embraces not only supernatural truths but also many natural ones, that is, those which could be known by the light of nature. Both points are clear from the Scriptures and from practice; and the reason is that the former truths cannot be known except through revelation, according to that of Matthew 16: Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, and the like; the latter, however, although they can in some way be known by natural light, as Paul witnesses in Romans 2, are nevertheless known by few; and therefore faith in them was necessary for the multitude of men — indeed even for the wise, so that they might hold those truths more firmly and certainly, which was also necessary so that they could firmly believe all the rest, as we shall see more fully in what follows; and thus it is also clear that in this entire matter of faith there is no other common note by which one could constitute a single adequate object of faith, except insofar as the whole of it stands, or can stand, immediately under divine revelation, by reason of which it has the same character of the credible — and thus the conclusion put forward is explained and proved.

div.head: Sectio 4
Utrum inter objecta complexa seu veritates credendas sit aliquis ordo
div.p: SECTION IV. Whether among the complex objects or truths to be believed there is any order?

1. The Ground for Doubt in this Question. — Since we have said in the preceding section that the material object of faith embraces several truths within itself, it is necessary to explain whether they have among themselves any order of prior and posterior; and the ground for doubt can be that where there is a multitude without order, there is confusion, and thus there could be no per se unity in the object of faith — and consequently none in faith itself — unless among the credible objects there were some order. On the contrary, however, it seems sufficient for this unity that all these credible things have an order toward the same formal character, and have their unity in that.

2. A Twofold Order among the Credible Things in the Order of Being and in the Order of the Credible. — The Order in the Order of Being: First, of Existence; Then, of Dignity. — To explain this, then, I note that these objects can be considered in two ways: first, in the order of being; second, in the order of the credible.
Then a manifold order can be conceived among them: namely, of existence, of dignity, of the relation of one to another, or of greater or lesser proportion and connaturality to faith itself, or finally of dependence or emanation of one from another. Speaking then of the credible things themselves according to themselves and according to their being, there is hardly any difficulty, because, as Scotus rightly said in book 3, distinction 23, it cannot be doubted that in this way there is some order among the credible things themselves. First, in being, because some are prior in existence to others — namely divine things to created, necessary to contingent, and eternal to temporal; for all these fall under this object, as we said. Second, they have an order of dignity in nearly the same way, because those that pertain to God are more worthy, as is clear. Here one can observe, among the propositions of faith, that some are such in which divine things are predicated of divine things, such as: God is Father, or omnipotent, and so forth; and these hold the first place of dignity, because both extremes are uncreated. Other propositions, however, are those in which created things are predicated of uncreated things, such as: God is man, or died, and the like; and among these can be counted those in which actions ad extra are predicated of God, for those actions are created and temporal, such as: God justifies, God creates, etc. And all these hold the second place of dignity, because they regard God himself proximately and contain his principal works and mysteries. There are also other propositions in which something uncreated is predicated of a created subject, such as: Man is God; but the same reasoning applies to these as to the preceding, because they differ only by conversion or transposition of the extremes. Finally there are other truths of faith in which a created thing is predicated of a created thing, such as: The soul is immortal; and these hold the lowest place, as is self-evident; and in each grade of these propositions great variety and inequality is found, as anyone can easily consider.

3. Tum denique habitudinis unius objecti ad
aliud. — Atque hinc constat esse etiam inter
has veritates ordinem habitudinis unius ad
allud; nam creata omnia ad divina ordinan
tur. Sicut enim supra dictum est, inter sub
jecta fidei incomplexa, Deum esse ad quem
caetera referuntur, ita veritates, quae Deum
ipsum spectant, primario intentae sunt, et re
liquae omnes ad illas ordinantur. Unde etiam
fit consequens ut respectu etiam ipsius fidei
habeant proportionatum ordinem; nam illa
quae sunt divina majorem proportionem ha
bent cum fide, quae supernaturalis etiam est,
et divina; unde fit ut ipsamet fides majorem
quamdam propensionem habeat ad divinas
veritates, quam ad reliquas, quia magis con
naturales illi sunt, ut sic dicam, et quia in
universum quaelibet virtus magis propensa est
in nobiliora, et meliora. Denique concluditur
ex dictis reperiri inter haec objecta ordinem
dependentiae, vel secundum se, vel in ordine
ad nos. Si enim creata ad divina comparen
tur, ab his pendent illa secundum veram cau
salitatem et realem; si vero comparentur di
vina inter se, sic habent ordinem in ordine
ad nos; sic enim concipimus Deum esse vo
lentem, quia est intelligens, et sic de aliis
attributis; qui ordo solet sufficere ad scien
tiam et demonstrationem, ac subinde ad con
nexionem rerum quae creduntur.

5. Second, More Probable Opinion, Affirming It. — Nevertheless, I consider it more probable that among the material objects of faith, even the complex ones, there is something, or some things, that must be believed first from the intrinsic nature of faith, and consequently that these are prior to others even in the mode of the credible. This was the teaching of Durandus, in book 3, distinction 24, question 4, and Palude there, question 1; and Almain, question 3; Marsilius, in book 3, question 14, article 1; and Vasquez held the same, in the first part, disputation 5, chapter 5, and it is commonly attributed to Thomas here, article 1, insofar as he says that the first truth is the reason for believing all other things that are believed through faith; though he does not explain whether he is speaking of the first truth as a quo principle, or also as something believed in a complex way as well. This must therefore be proved by argument. And first we grant to the previous opinion what it asserted in its third argument, namely, that among the purely material objects of faith there is no per se order, as that third argument rightly proves, and the second argument of the previous opinion as well. We therefore establish an order only between the material and the formal, even insofar as the formal is itself something believed. And this is proved and explained, first, by analogy with human faith; for human faith depends upon two principles that must necessarily be known beforehand if anything is to be believed on someone's authority: one is that this person says it; the other is that this person is worthy of belief; hence also in the schools, when we argue from someone's authority, we first carefully inquire whether he actually says this, and then we emphasize his authority or presuppose it as
known. Therefore in human faith those are, as it were, two first principles upon which the other credible things depend in the mode of the credible; therefore the same must be said proportionally of divine faith; for they agree in the essential character of faith and differ only in the authority of the one testifying.

6. An Evasion. — One can reply that in human faith those two principles are indeed presupposed, but not as believed on the authority of the same person to whom faith is given regarding other matters; rather, they are known either through experience — because I hear the person speaking, or read his writings — or through an opinion I form about his authority from other indications. And thus, staying precisely within the character of human faith with respect to such a person, those principles are not first credible things, nor is any order to be found among the credible things. Some reason about infused faith in this same way; for they grant that it presupposes these two principles: God said this, and: God cannot deceive — but not as known through infused faith itself, but from elsewhere: the first through the human testimony of those who propose the faith, such as through the preaching of the Apostles and the miracles they performed, etc.; the second through natural evidence, since it is evident that God is the first and infallible truth, who cannot deceive. And thus those principles stand outside the character of things credible through faith, and therefore, though they are prior in themselves, nonetheless among the credible things themselves there is no order.

7. Refutation. — Nevertheless, although divine and human faith agree in this, that each is grounded in those two principles as adapted to itself, they differ greatly in the kind of knowledge of such principles that each requires. For human faith is uncertain and fallible, and therefore can presuppose those principles as known in a more perfect way, or at least in a way no less perfect; and thus it often presupposes the testimony of the speaker as evidently known as regards the act of testifying itself; and the truthfulness of the one testifying it likewise presupposes as known, either through another human faith, or through the testimony of another person, or through conjecture and opinion no less probable than the faith generated from it. Divine faith, however, is infallibly certain — indeed more certain than any natural knowledge, as I shall show below — and therefore it cannot rest per se and formally upon those principles as known by any other natural knowledge; for if
that knowledge is human faith, it is imperfect. Hence whoever believes God to be triune because God said so must believe that God said it just as certainly as that God is triune; therefore human faith in the proposition: God said this — even if confirmed by the testimony of very many people and by human arguments — does not suffice, because it is always uncertain, especially in comparison with divine faith. And by the same reasoning, it does not suffice that the other proposition: God is the first truth who cannot deceive, be known by natural light alone; for even that knowledge is less certain, so much so that there have been theologians who have doubted it; therefore it is impossible that the first truth known only in that way should ground the certain assent of infused faith, since a building cannot be more solid than its foundation, just as a conclusion cannot be more certain than its principle. From this it is concluded that those principles must be known by a supernatural light; and in this life there is no supernatural light prior to or better than faith, speaking according to the ordinary and general rule; therefore those two principles are the foundation of faith in no other way than as known through faith itself; therefore in the mode of the credible by divine faith, they are prior to the other credible things, which depend on them under that character.

8. The Evasion Pressed Further. — Confirmed. — Others reply, however, that those two principles — God said this, and: God cannot deceive — are included in every credible thing through faith insofar as it is such, but they are not necessarily presupposed per se as known as objects (ut quod), but only as a means (ut quo), or as the reason for believing; and thus, insofar as they are among the credible things, they are not prior, since they are not necessarily known first. The assumption is explained as follows: one who believes God to be triune because he said so believes this truth — God is triune — by a single act, and attends only to God's saying it as the reason for believing. For this is how simple believers believe, and they do not distinguish multiple credible things there. Indeed it does not even seem necessary that divine revelation directly bear upon both, but only upon the truth itself that is believed; for by the very fact that God reveals himself to be triune, he says that he says it, and no other revelation is necessary; and still less does a revelation of the other proposition — God is truthful — seem necessary, since this too is virtually included in any testimony of God: for if such testimony is such as to oblige belief in God, by that very fact, and as it were in the exercise of the act, it obliges belief that God is truthful in that testimony. And this is confirmed: for it is not necessary that in every assent of the intellect the reason for assenting be known reflectively and as an object (ut quod); for in assenting to first principles, natural light is the reason for assenting, and yet it is not foreknown in that way. Indeed there are those who think the same holds in human faith as well, namely, that it gives assent to the thing said on the basis of a person's testimony considered only as the reason for assenting, even though it is not thought of as a known object.

9. Refutation of What Was Said in the Preceding Evasion. — But this opinion cannot be approved by me; for I do not understand how something that is not truly known by the intellect can be a reason for assenting. To remove equivocation, however, one must note that the discussion here concerns the formal objective reason, not the principle of assenting on the part of the intellect; for speaking of this latter principle, it is clear that it is not necessary for the object to be known first, as is evident from species and from the cognitive power itself. And therefore the example of assenting to first principles is not to the point, because there the light of the intellect is the principle or reason for assenting only on the part of the power; for on the part of the object, the reason for assenting is the immediate connection of the terms and the truth that shines forth in it. Here, however, we are not treating of the reason for assenting on the part of the intellect — for this is the light of faith itself, which we also grant need not be foreknown as an object — but we are treating of the reason for knowing on the part of the object; for since the truths of faith are not self-evident to believers, the reason for believing cannot be the immediate connection of terms or the truth of the thing in itself, since this is not seen by the intellect; and therefore another reason is needed upon which the assent is grounded, and that reason is the testimony of God. Regarding this reason, then, we say it is necessary that it be presupposed as known and believed as a certain revealed truth, because it is impossible for the intellect to be moved and drawn to assent by a thing or medium of assenting that it does not know, since it is moved only through cognition; just as in the will it is impossible for any object or its goodness to move the will without being foreknown — so much more is it necessary in the intellect that the medium which moves it to assent be foreknown by it.

10. The Refutation Corroborated. — Nor is the difficulty of this argument avoided by that distinction between an object known as a means (ut quo) or as an object (ut quod), and by saying that the formal reason for assenting in faith is known as a means (ut quo) but not as an
object (ut quod). For I ask: does being known as a means (ut quo) constitute being truly known, such that the intellect assents that it is so, as is necessary for a motive of believing? For if this is not truly known, the argument already made presses: that it is impossible for such a reason to be a motive inclining and drawing the intellect to assent. But if all of that is truly known regarding such a medium, it is falsely said not to be an object (ut quod), because it terminates the cognition of the mind in itself, and this is an object (ut quod). And this is finally clarified as follows: the intellect does not assent through faith to the truths that are material objects of faith as self-evident from knowledge of the terms, since it does not see the terms as they are in themselves; therefore it must know their connection through some medium, and that medium is nothing other than divine revelation and truth; therefore it is necessary that the intellect know that medium properly and in itself, and consequently it is also necessary that it know that such a medium truly applies to the given object or matter, and that it has the property necessary to render that object infallibly credible; and this is nothing other than knowing that the revelation or testimony of God is infallible and bears upon such an object as something said by God.

11. Reply to the Objection in Number 8. — Hence the objection just made is easily answered: it is true that one cannot believe God to be triune and one unless one believes that this was said by God, whether this is done by distinct acts or by one; for perhaps it can happen either way. I think, however, that at the beginning of believing, when faith is generated, it happens by distinct acts: first one arrives at believing that this was said by God, and then one believes what was said; but afterward, in virtue of preceding acts, it can happen that the whole is apprehended at once and believed by one act — just as with a scientific conclusion, it customarily happens that one must first know expressly the middle term by which the extremes are joined, but afterward, from habit, the intellect assents to it by a single simple act. Nor does it matter that both that it is God who speaks and what he says are proposed by one revelation or utterance of God; for this does not prevent them from being distinct credible propositions, which the human mind — especially one beginning the assent of faith — cannot apprehend so simply and by one act, and therefore must first know the one that is the reason for knowing the other. And the same must be said proportionally of the other proposition: God is the first infallible
truth, or: God cannot lie; for the very utterance of God is not efficacious for grounding the assent of faith except in virtue of this truth, and therefore this too must be foreknown. Nor does it suffice to say that by believing something because God said it, one necessarily believes that God does not lie; for granted that one believes this of that particular act or object, it is necessary that it be grounded in the universal judgment that God can never lie, and thus that he is in himself an infallible truth. And the same holds proportionally in human faith (in which a great equivocation seems to be committed). For though by believing something to someone I believe that he does not lie in it, nevertheless this faith necessarily presupposes a credence or estimate about such a person — that he is not accustomed to lying, or that he is worthy of such faith; and so it is proportionally in the present case. As for the evident knowledge of first principles through the natural light of the intellect, the reasoning is not similar; because there the light of the intellect is not a medium or reason for knowing on the part of the object, but only on the part of the power; rather the reason for knowing on the part of the object is the immediate connection of terms, which the intellect sees once the terms are known — which is not the case here, as we have explained.

13. Reply to the Second Foundation, ibid. — And to the Third. — To the second argument, about the immediate relation of divine revelation to all credible objects, the reply is that this is true of purely material objects, but not of the formal and material compared with each other. And this is why I said in section one that God is a necessary object of faith, because he cannot sufficiently reveal other things without revealing himself — at least those properties necessary for faith to be given to him. And therefore it is no obstacle that God freely reveals what he wills; for given that he wills to reveal something as to be believed on his authority, it is necessary that he propose himself as the one revealing and worthy of faith. The third argument, moreover, is resolved from what has been said: for we granted that among purely material objects there is no order; but between the formal and the material it cannot be denied, even insofar as the formal object itself can be known in a complex way and thus be one of the material objects known.

14. A Small Question Appended to What Has Been Said. — Its Resolution. — Someone will ask: since two propositions to be believed by faith are formed about the formal object — namely: God has spoken the things of faith, and: God could not be a false witness — whether there is an order between them, and which of them is prior. Likewise, since each of them presupposes another — namely, that God exists — whether this should be placed first. I reply briefly that in the order of reality these truths do indeed have an order; for that God exists is presupposed for everything, and that he is truthful is a universal and necessary property, and thus prior to any particular divine revelation. Nevertheless, in the mode of the credible, they so mutually include each other or depend upon each other that they do not appear to have among themselves an order of prior and posterior in the mode of the credible: for it is not credible through faith that God says something unless it rests upon divine truthfulness; nor is it credible through the same faith that God is truthful, except insofar as it has been said or revealed by God — and so these two mutually support each other. As for that God exists, it is included in each of them and is not presupposed per se in any way in order for the rest to be believed.

div.head: Sectio 5
Utrum materia fidei convenienter in symbolo fidei tradatur
div.p: SECTION V. Whether the matter of faith is fittingly handed down in the Symbol of faith?

1. The Etymology of the Symbol and Its Use in the Church. — The Symbol, as all presuppose in this matter, is a Greek word, signifying sign or indication and collection, as in military service, for example, the sign that is given to soldiers so that they may recognize one another and be distinguished from others is called a symbol. Also the collection that is customarily made from many contributors for some work is also accustomed to be called a symbol. And from both significations this word has been applied by the Church to signify a certain brief summary or rule of faith, collected from various articles of faith, and proposed to the faithful as the sign of their profession. Concerning this symbol, therefore, which Clement, in the Letter to James, Augustine, sermon 125 on the season, Cyprian, and Ruffinus, in the exposition of the symbol, and other Fathers explain, all theologians in Book 3, distinction 25 dispute in common, and especially St. Thomas here, articles 6, 8, and 9, and therefore the rationale of this symbol must be briefly explained by us, especially since Luther also criticizes this custom in the Church, because for believing (he says) Scripture sufficed, without the addition of the Symbol.

2. A Note from St. Thomas for the Resolution. — In order to explain the truth, St. Thomas notes that among the matter of faith some things are handed down per se, because faith is the substance of things hoped for, and therefore those things which pertain to the beatitude that we hope for, or are necessary means, or are ordered per se to attaining it, are said to pertain per se to faith; the rest, however, which are innumerable, are revealed as it were by occasion or per accidens, and thus the entire matter of faith embraces both orders of credible things. Speaking therefore of the matter of faith in this universality, it is clear that it neither ought to have been, nor could it practically have been, proposed under a brief symbol, because thus all things that are in Scripture pertain to the matter of faith, and not only those, but also what is held by tradition and the definition of the Church, all of which could neither be reduced to a brief summary, nor was this necessary for the Christian people. Therefore in the present case there is discussion only of the matter per se, and especially of that which is necessary for salvation.

3. First Assertion Concerning Faith. — Proved by Induction. —
In How Many Ways the Symbol Could Have Been Composed by the Apostles. — When It Was Composed. — For What Reasons They Composed It. — I say first, that it was most fitting for the Church to make a symbol embracing the matter of faith of this kind. This is a matter of faith from perpetual tradition and the common consent of the Church, and it is proved first of all by induction; for the first symbol was handed down to us by the Apostles, which is called the Apostles' Creed, as Clement, Letter 1 to James testifies, and Book 1 of the Recognitions; Pope Leo, Letter 13 to Pulcheria, and sermon 3 on the Passion of the Lord; Augustine, sermons 115 and 181 on the Seasons, elsewhere in the Appendix, sermons 42 and 57, and the book on Faith and the Symbol, and often elsewhere; and Jerome, Letter 61 to Pammachius; Ambrose, sermon 38; and Chrysostom, homilies 1 and 2 on the Symbol, and others to be cited shortly. Tertullian, however, in the book on the Prescription of Heretics, chapter 14, says that the Symbol was instituted by Christ; but this must be understood as through the Apostles, because it is not established, nor can it be affirmed with any foundation, that Christ himself composed this Symbol in the manner and order in which it has always been retained in the Church. Now this Symbol could have been composed in two ways: either because both the whole and its individual parts were collected and approved by all the Apostles together, or because individual Apostles contributed individual articles and sentences. And although it is uncertain in which of these ways it was composed, the Fathers point to the latter, especially Clement and Augustine, who relates that individual sentences were contributed by individual Apostles; and Pope Leo says thus: The brief and perfect confession of the Catholic symbol is marked by the sentences of the twelve Apostles, and nearly the same is found in Isidore, Book 1 of the Divine Offices, chapter 16, and Book 2, chapter 22. From this we also understand that this Symbol was composed by the Apostles before the death of James, for he too contributed his sentence, as the said Fathers note; and so Baronius, in volume 1, year 44, thinks it was composed in that year, that is, the tenth year after the Passion of Christ. And this is consonant with what the Fathers say in the cited places: that the Apostles composed the Symbol when they wished to separate from one another and be distributed throughout the whole world. And from this they also gather the reasons for which they composed it: first, so that they might have one and the same
rule of faith, which all might propose to all peoples: so Ruffinus in the preface to the symbol. Second, so that individual faithful might have a brief formula of faith, which they could retain in memory and profess daily and frequently; so Augustine, homily 42, and in the sermon on the Symbol. Third, so that the faithful might be protected from false preachers who intended to corrupt the faith: so Chrysostom, homily on the Apostles' Creed. From this the said Fathers also note that the Apostles did not hand down the Symbol written on paper and ink, lest it could be corrupted by heretics, but handed it down by word alone, so that it might be retained in the heart, as besides those cited Peter Chrysologus, sermon 57 and the following sermons on the Symbol often repeats; and Eusebius of Emesa, homilies 1 and 2 on the Symbol, and most excellently Ruffinus, in the Exposition of the Symbol.

4. Those Who Doubted Whether the Symbol Was Composed by the Apostles Were in Error. — The Foundation of the Error Is Refuted in Multiple Ways. — From these things, therefore, it is sufficiently concluded that some who profess themselves Catholics gravely erred in calling into doubt whether this symbol is apostolic, since they could have had no reason for doubting against so many Fathers and the universal tradition of the Church. But they say: if this Symbol was composed by the Apostles, then it is canonical Scripture; for if a letter written by one Apostle is canonical Scripture, why not the Symbol composed by all of them. It is easily replied, however, by denying the inference; first, because although it is certain that this Symbol is apostolic, it is nevertheless not simply a matter of faith, nor has it been defined by the Church. Second, because although the Apostles handed it down, with the Holy Spirit governing and directing the truth of the sentences, he did not however dictate the individual words, which is necessary for canonical Scripture. Third, because the Church does not receive it among the canonical Scriptures. Fourth, because we said, from the teaching of the Fathers, that the symbol itself was not written by the Apostles, but handed down orally, so that it might be preserved in the memories of the faithful, as Augustine, sermon 119 on the Seasons also thought; how then could it be Sacred Scripture? Indeed, from this a powerful argument is drawn against the heretics who believe in canonical Scriptures alone — for from this we have that apostolic tradition suffices to show that Scripture alone does not. Moreover, what some say — that the Apostles collected the Symbol from the Scriptures — is to be understood in a sound sense; both because something is contained in that Symbol which is not found in Scripture, namely that Christ descended into hell;
and also because that Symbol is older than the writings of the New Testament, from which it could chiefly have been drawn: therefore it could be said in a broad sense to be taken from Scripture, because it contains in substance the same mysteries that are handed down in Scripture.

5. The Stated Assertion Proceeds Also Concerning the Symbol Enriched in Various Councils. — Also Concerning the Symbol of Athanasius. — Other Symbols Are Reduced to the Aforementioned Ones. — The second Symbol is the Nicene, or Constantinopolitan, which St. Thomas here called the Symbol of the Fathers, because it was not completed in one Council, but was begun in the Nicene Council, then augmented and more fully declared in the Constantinopolitan, and afterwards also approved in the First Council of Ephesus, and moreover after these Councils it received some addition — as we said concerning that clause, "and the Son" (Filioque), in Book 10 on the Trinity, chapter 1, numbers 15 and following, where we also noted that it is not altogether certain at what time, or by which Pontiff or Council, it was added, although by certain faith it is established that it was rightly added; and thus we also say now that it is not established when that Symbol was completed in every respect, as it is now sung in the Church; it is certain, however, that it too is an infallible rule of faith, confirmed by the authority of the Church and the Supreme Pontiffs. The third symbol is that of Athanasius; for they greatly err who dare to deny that it was composed by Athanasius, since Gregory Nazianzen, in his oration in praise of Athanasius, says that Athanasius wrote an outstanding confession of his faith, nor does he undeservedly call it a confession and not a Symbol, because Athanasius, since he was not the Supreme Pontiff but a particular bishop, could not hand down an authentic symbol of the Church, as St. Thomas said here, article 3, ad 3; nevertheless, since it has now been approved by the Church, it is rightly numbered among the symbols, and so Pope Eugenius, in the Council of Florence, in the Decree for the Armenians, chapter six handed down the Symbol of Athanasius to them as a rule of faith, and Augustine often uses it to confirm the truths of faith, and specifically on Psalm 120 reports it under the name of Athanasius. Besides these symbols, moreover, various propositions of faith are found in almost all Councils, which in sum contain the matter of faith; all of these, however, are reduced to the aforementioned symbols, as can be seen especially in the Sixth Council of Carthage, chapter 10, and in the Eleventh Council of Toledo, at the beginning.

8. Objection Against the Proximate Assertion. — Confirmed First. — Confirmed Second. —
But someone will object: for either this sufficiency exists in each individual symbol, and so multiple symbols are multiplied superfluously, or it exists only in their collection, and thus the individual ones are insufficient, which cannot be said. And the difficulty is increased, because in one symbol some things are omitted that are contained in another: as in the Apostles' Symbol the descent of Christ to hell and the communion of saints are placed, which are omitted in the Nicene Symbol; and conversely in the Symbol of the Fathers the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father is placed, which is omitted in the Apostolic, and in the same [Apostolic Symbol] the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son was afterwards added, which had previously been omitted. And what presses more urgently: since Paul says that first of all one must believe that God exists and that he is a rewarder, neither of these is placed in the symbols. And finally the mystery of the Eucharist seems most necessary to believe, and is one of the more difficult mysteries, and yet it is not placed in the symbols; therefore there is not a sufficiency of doctrine in the symbols.

9. Replies to the Objections. — The Threefold End of the Symbol. — To the First Confirmation. — To the Second Confirmation. — The reply to the principal difficulty is given, with Alexander of Hales, 3rd part, question 69, member 2, that the ends of each individual symbol must be considered, and thus each is sufficient for its own end, and all together are sufficient for all the ends taken together. Now these ends are three: namely, the instruction of the faithful, the refutation of heresies, and the greater explanation of the mysteries. For the first end the Apostles' Symbol was instituted, and for that end it is most sufficient; for if the faithful know and believe what is contained in it, it suffices for salvation. For the second end, namely the refutation of errors, the Symbol of the Fathers, or of the Councils, was instituted — as I think — although Alexander of Hales attributes this to the Symbol of Athanasius; yet it is in fact clear that this was the aim of the Nicene Council and those that followed; and thus if anyone pays careful attention, he will find that the individual clauses added to this Symbol beyond the Apostolic were aimed at refuting individual heresies, especially against the mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation, as Gabriel, distinction 25, question 1 discusses; Athanasius, however, composed his Symbol for a greater explanation of these mysteries, and therefore in it he added many things and omitted almost everything else. And from this the other difficulty is easily resolved: for those two articles concerning the communion of saints and the descent into hell were omitted in the Symbol of the
Fathers, either because no heresies had arisen concerning them, or perhaps because it is not necessary for individual faithful to believe these more explicitly than they are contained in the articles concerning the death of Christ and the holiness and unity of the Church, as I treated in part in the 2nd volume of the third part, disputation 43, and in part we shall see below, treating the precepts of faith in the 2nd moral part, disputation 13, section 6. As for the confirmation concerning the existence and providence of God, St. Thomas indicates that these things which can be known by natural light concerning God are not placed in faith but presupposed. And it can rightly be said that God's existence is sufficiently taught at the beginning of the Symbol, when we say we believe in one God the Father Almighty, for if God is one, he most certainly exists; and that God is a rewarder is sufficiently and specifically contained in the article on the future judgment and on eternal life. Finally, concerning the mystery of the Eucharist, St. Thomas, II-II, question 1, article 8, ad 6 says it was comprehended under the omnipotence of God or under the mystery of the Incarnation; but this is very implicit, since that mystery must nevertheless be believed explicitly, as I said in disputation 46 on the Sacraments, section 1, at the end, and therefore I add that what was placed in the symbols are things that pertain per se to the knowledge of God and Christ, for the sake of the perfection and obedience of the intellect, and for strengthening hope and exciting charity; but beyond those things it is necessary to know and believe many other things for the sake of acting, which were not placed in the symbols; and therefore beyond the symbols, knowledge of the commandments is necessary, to which belongs instruction about the necessary sacraments, one of which is the Eucharist, as also knowledge of the Lord's Prayer.

10. First Assertion: The Symbol Rightly Consists of Articles. — An Article Adds More Than a Proposition of Faith. — I say third, that the Symbol of faith is aptly and fittingly composed of articles of faith. I set forth this assertion in order to explain the name "article of faith" and the number of the articles, because on this many things are written by theologians, as can be seen in St. Thomas, and Alexander of Hales, in the cited places, Scotus, and Gabriel, in Book 3, distinction 25, first question. All agree, therefore, that not every proposition of faith is an article of faith, although conversely every article of faith is a proposition of faith to be believed. What it adds, first of all, is that it pertains per se to faith; but this too is common to many other propositions which are not articles of faith. St. Thomas therefore adds that for an article of faith it is necessary that it have a special difficulty, and consequently he distinguishes articles by the special difficulties of credible things, which is probable. Others, however, think that an article is a special proposition of faith pertaining per se to faith, which must be believed explicitly; and perhaps this is what Richard of St. Victor meant, whom Alexander of Hales cites above, member 5, when he said that an article is an indivisible proposition of faith constraining us to believe. Others, finally, think that an article is nothing other than a clause of faith approved by some Apostle for the composition of the Symbol, according to what we reported above from Clement and Augustine; and thus for the distinction of articles a distinct relationship to its author suffices, along with some usefulness accruing to the faithful from the distinction of such sentences; and each of these explanations suffices, since it is more a matter of the signification of the word than of the thing itself. From this it is also clear what must be said about the number of articles; for if they are distinguished with respect to the first authors of the Symbol, there will be twelve articles, just as there were twelve Apostles — for Paul and Barnabas were not present there; and so think Augustine above, and Pope Leo, in the said thirteenth letter, and sermon eleven on the Passion, chapter two. But if they are distinguished by the difficulty of credible things, or by the distinction of mysteries, then fourteen are rightly distinguished, as is the common distinction that the Scholastics are accustomed to approve, with St. Thomas in that eighth article, especially Gabriel and Scotus above; and these too suffice for the proof of the conclusion: for from the tenor of the symbol it is clear that in it the mysteries of faith are openly explained through various sentences or clauses, insofar as was fitting for the explicit faith of the faithful; and the order of these, although it might seem to be somewhat inverted by proposing first the mysteries of the humanity of Christ before the mysteries of the divinity of the Holy Spirit, was nevertheless most apt, both for the sake of greater brevity and for the sake of signifying more fully the unity of the person of Christ as God and man.

11. A Two-Part Doubt. — The Second Member. — There remains one doubt only: how all the faithful can profess that they believe in God [credere in Deum], since not all have formed faith; but that phrase, in Deum, as toward the ultimate end loved above all things, indicates a movement of faith toward God, as St. Thomas, following Augustine, teaches below, question 2, article 2. From this it is also more difficult to explain that in the Symbol the faithful are said to believe in the holy Church,
although the Church is a creature; and thus indeed Epiphanius, in the Ancoratus, near the end reads it, reporting the Symbol of the Fathers, which he says is held by the Church; in the same way Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis 18 reads it, and says that that phrase is placed in the symbol so that the faithful may flee the conventicles of heretics and persevere in the Catholic Church, in which they were reborn; and Jerome, in the Dialogue against the Luciferians seems to speak in the same way, and it is also reported from Augustine, in chapter 1 on Consecration, distinction 4.

12. St. Thomas's Reply to the First Member. — An Easier Reply. — To the prior part St. Thomas replies that the faithful, through the symbol, profess the faith of the entire Catholic Church, and because the Church always believes in God with formed faith, although not each individual member of the Church always believes thus — since not all members of the Church are just, although the just never fail in the Church — for whose sake the Church is said to believe in God with formed faith, and therefore this is proposed in the symbol to individual faithful. This is probably stated; but since each individual faithful person, when professing the faith, speaks not in the person of the Church but in his own, it seems necessary that those words be able to be said truly by individual faithful in their own person, even if they are in a state of sin. Hence it can more easily be said that that phrase, in Deum, does not always denote the disposition of formed faith, but it suffices that it denote the disposition toward the principal object of faith, or also toward the ultimate end which is lovable above all things, even if it is perhaps not actually loved by the one believing. For thus we read in John 12, concerning certain ones: And they believed in him, namely in Christ, of whom it is immediately added: they did not confess him, because they loved the glory of men more than God; and in 1 John 5 we are said to believe in the testimony of God, that is, in his testimony.

13. Reply to the Second Member. — Erasmus to Be Avoided. — And from this a reply can be given to the other part, by admitting that reading — to believe in the one and holy Church — does not signify a disposition toward the ultimate end, but either only toward the object believed, so that to believe in the holy Church is nothing other than to believe that it is one and holy, or at most it is to believe in it as the infallible rule of faith, witnessing and proposing [the faith] from the movement of the Holy Spirit. In this regard the manner of speaking of Erasmus, in the dialogue on Faith must be avoided, where he says he does not believe in the Church, because it is a congregation of men which can deceive; for although the Church, as it consists of men,
could from this standpoint be deceived and deceive, yet insofar as it is governed by the Holy Spirit, it is the pillar and foundation of truth, 1 Tim. 2. Thus then it could be said in a good sense: I believe in the Church, just as in Exod. 14: They believed in God and in Moses; and in the Hebrew it has: In God and in Moses; and in Psalm 70: They did not believe in his wonders. Nevertheless the truth is that in the Symbol one does not have Credo in sanctam, but Credo sanctam Ecclesiam, so that it is the thing believed, not the reason or end of believing, and thus it is commonly found in the Symbol of the Church and in the Councils, and Augustine admonishes this in sermon 115 on the Seasons, and chapter 12, and the book on Faith and the Symbol, chapter 10, and another passage cited from the Decree in the Gregorian Code has been corrected; and Marius Victorinus also corrected the readings of Jerome according to older and more reliable codices; so also read Eusebius of Emesa, sermons 1 and 2 on the Symbol; Ruffinus, Chrysologus, and others who write on the symbol, while Epiphanius and Cyril do not seem to have distinguished so carefully between those words with the particle in or without it, and therefore seem to have written thus.

div.head: Section 6
Whether the matter of faith has grown over the course of time, or has at times been diminished
div.p: SECTION VI. Whether the matter of faith has grown over the course of time, or has at times been diminished.

1. The Sense of the Question Explained. — Three Periods of the Church. — In this question, just as in the preceding one, we speak of the matter of faith per se; for in accidental matters change can easily occur, as we shall also see. But the essential matter of faith is entirely reducible to knowledge of the mysteries of God, as he is God, and of Christ, as he is redeemer, according to that saying: This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent; and thus the sense of the question is whether this knowledge of God and Christ was greater or lesser in different times or ages of the Church. To explain this, three principal periods of the Church must be distinguished, namely, the age of the natural law, the written law, and the law of grace; and within each of those periods various times can also be considered, as Gregory, in his Homilies on the Gospels, distinguishes the age of the natural law from the beginning up to the flood, and from Noah up to Abraham, and from Abraham up to Moses. Likewise, in each of these ages one must distinguish those men who were the leaders and pastors of the Church in their times from the common people and laity of the Church, and thus
various comparisons arise concerning the perfections of faith, which we shall briefly explain.

2.
