Two Modes of Believing: Explicitly and Implicitly. — The Mode of Believing Explicitly Varies Only by More and Less. — The Mode of Believing Implicitly Varies from Various Principles. — First. — Second. — Third. — Fourth. — I further suppose that two modes are distinguished by which the matter of faith can be believed, namely, explicitly and implicitly, a distinction which will serve for nearly the whole of the matter. To believe explicitly is nothing other than to believe something in itself, so that it is the proximate object upon which the assent of faith falls. But to believe implicitly is to believe only in another thing; for what is thus believed is in truth not known, nor does the intellect form its own concept of the proposition that is said to be believed only implicitly, but rather of the other proposition in which it is contained. And the former mode varies only by more and less, insofar as a more or less perfect concept can be formed about the same mystery of faith, or also insofar as more or fewer things can be known about the same thing believed. If one considers rightly, however, this variety consists only either in more acts of faith, by which more truths pertaining to the same mystery or to the same thing believed are believed explicitly and in themselves; or certainly, if there is greater or lesser expression regarding the very same truth, the diversity lies more in the apprehension than in the assent of faith itself, and thus it can arise from human learning and effort through acquired science, or through a better intellect or better intelligible species. But the latter mode — namely, of implicit faith — can be founded on various principles. For first, in one thing believed explicitly, other things can be said to be believed implicitly by reason of the formal object, in which all believable things are connected, so that it is impossible to believe one thing because God has revealed it without the soul being disposed to believe all revealed things, if they are sufficiently proposed, and for this reason they are believed implicitly; just as, on the contrary, one who denies one article of faith implicitly denies all, because he cannot adhere to others through faith if he departs from one; or just as one who explicitly detests one sin on account of God implicitly detests all by force and implication. Second, this implicit faith can exist by relation to others who believe explicitly; for in this way the simple faithful are said to believe all that the Church believes, or what the Apostles handed down, even though they are ignorant of those things. Third, this can occur on the part of the matter itself, and that in many ways, namely, either because one proposition is contained in another as a conclusion in a principle, from which it can be evidently drawn — and in this way, one who believes that Christ is a man implicitly believes that he is visible; or because one proposition is connected with another in the thing itself, or through the identity of the thing, although the connection itself cannot be known without faith — and in this way, one who believes that God is infinite implicitly believes that he is triune; or also, a particular is known implicitly in a universal, as is self-evident. And finally, the circumstances of a mystery are said to be known implicitly in its substance, and so one who believes that Christ is the redeemer implicitly believes that he died for men, and the like.

6. Second Assertion. — The Assertion is Supported by Authority. — Also Supported by Reason. — Second, it must be said that this faith has always been explicit in the Church. This assertion too is taught by the theologians cited, and it is understood principally of the faith of men; for we discuss the faith of Angels in book five on Angels, chapter six, although both assertions can be verified of it as well; for wayfaring Angels also tended through faith toward the same beatitude as men, and through the same Christ, as the more probable opinion holds; and therefore they also had explicit faith in the Trinity and the Incarnation, as is treated in the first part, question fifty-seven, and as I said in volume 1 on the Incarnation, disputation 32. The assertion is also understood principally of fallen men, for the state of innocence is treated elsewhere; but since it will be necessary to explain the assertion, I suppose that Adam also in the state of innocence had explicit faith in Christ and his Incarnation. I proved this at length in part 3, question 1, in the Commentary on article 3, from the common teaching of the Fathers, and it is now a commonly received opinion. From this it is thus credible in itself that Adam taught and handed on this faith to his sons, and so it was preserved by tradition in the Church of the faithful, even with respect to explicit faith in Christ; whence Pope Leo, Letter 23, says that from the beginning of the human race it was announced to men that Christ would come in the flesh; and Bernard, sermon 6 on the Vigil of the Nativity, says that prophecy about Christ took its beginning from Adam himself. Whence Job had this faith, when in chapter 19 he said: I know that my Redeemer lives; from which Augustine, book 18 of the City of God, chapter 57, also infers that this faith was preserved among some of the gentiles. Whence also the sacrifices which the faithful then offered are believed to have been some signification of the Christ to come, for which reason it is said in Revelation: the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world, as many expound it; and from Hebrews 7, it is established that Melchisedech offered sacrifice as a figure of Christ. But later, when this faith had been obscured by sins and men began to decline toward idolatry, it was renewed in Abraham, who had a more express faith in the mysteries, according to that of John 8: Abraham rejoiced to see my day; he saw it, and was glad, and afterwards through the hands of the Fathers and through the frequent revelations of God made to Isaac, Jacob, and others, it came down to Moses, of whom, before he received the law, Paul says in Hebrews 11: by faith, he preferred the reproach of Christ to the treasures of Egypt; and afterwards, in Exodus 6, there is narrated an excellent knowledge of God communicated to him. David also had this faith very expressly, as is evident from his Psalms and from the words of Christ in Matthew 22: David in spirit calls him Lord; and the same is true of the other Prophets, especially Isaiah, of whom it is said in John 12: that he saw the glory of God, and spoke of him; and in Luke 10 it is said generally that many kings and Prophets desired to see him; whence also, in Genes. 19, it is said: the desired one of all nations. From which Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 24, rightly concludes: If they desired, therefore they believed in him, which desires lasted until aged Simeon; but for the later period of the Church the matter is clear. The argument from reason is none other than this: it was so ordained and provided by God for his own glory and that of Christ, that he might be more perfectly believed and loved by the faithful Church; likewise because it was fitting that the principal mysteries of God, which are to be seen in the homeland, should always be explicitly believed by men on the way.

5. Third Assertion, in Two Parts. — The First Part on What Basis It Stands. — The Second Part Shown by Authority. — I say thirdly: this explicit faith was always present in the Church in its heads or leaders, but in the common people it was for the most part absent until the age of the law of grace. This assertion too is clear, and the first part has just been proved in the preceding assertion; for what we adduced proves it especially of the leaders of the Church. But the other part can be drawn from that passage in Ephesians 3: which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations, that is, to the common people, where Salmerón, Justinianus, and Cornelius, our commentators, note this from certain Fathers, weighing also what follows: as it has now been revealed to the holy Apostles, etc., as if to say, it was far more obscure formerly to ordinary men than it is now. Whence John, first canonical epistle, chapter five: We know that the Son of God has come, and has given us understanding, that we may know the true God, and be in his true Son; whence Gregory, homily 16 on Ezekiel, a little past the middle: The knowledge (he says) that was in the spiritual Fathers was not known to the whole people of the Hebrews; for when the Prophets preached the omnipotent God — namely, the holy Trinity — the people were ignorant of it, holding only the Decalogue in faith, not knowing the law of the Trinity. This view holds true with much greater reason in the Church of the Gentiles, which existed before the written law, or even alongside it. Indeed, the people of God surpassed in this, because it had a more express knowledge of God himself; for the oracles of God were entrusted to it, Romans 4. It was also obliged to believe explicitly that the Messiah would come, to which the Gentiles were not obliged, because it was not proposed to them in that way. Yet not even the people of the Hebrews recognized the Trinity, nor was the divinity of the coming Messiah explicitly proposed to them; nor were the other specific mysteries of him, all of which the Christian people now believes explicitly, as is evident from what was said about the Symbol. The argument from reason for this truth also depends principally on divine ordination; the fittingness on the part of men is given because those states of men were imperfect, according to that of Hebrews 7: the law brought nothing to perfection. Likewise because the human race was in a state of enmity, inasmuch as satisfaction had not been made to God for the common offense; and therefore, until the presence of Christ, knowledge of faith, like the other gifts of grace, was not communicated to men with great abundance, but only as much as was expedient
for the greater glory of Christ and for the execution of divine predestination.

6. Fourth Assertion, which Formally Answers the Title. — Its Argument. — Fourth, from this a response is gathered to the proposed question, namely that the matter of faith, with respect to explicit faith, has grown over the course of time. I say with respect to explicit faith, because implicit faith was always present, and in all persons, concerning the whole matter of faith, through some of the modes of implicit faith enumerated above, as each one will easily be able to see by applying them. Concerning explicit faith, however, it is easily established from what has been said. The argument is that through various times divine revelations and prophecies were multiplied, by which the doctrine and matter of faith was proposed more expressly to men, as is evident from Scripture, and as St. Thomas teaches at length in 2.2, q.174, art. 6. There remains a difficulty, however, in explaining how this growth is to be understood and what rule is to be observed in it; for two rules are handed down by the Fathers, which are not without difficulty.

8. A Dilemma Against the Said Rule. — The First Part of the Dilemma is Refuted. — The Second Part of the Dilemma. — It is Argued Against It. — Second Rule from St. Gregory. — Fittingness for the Second Rule. — This rule, however, is not without difficulty: for it is understood either universally or indefinitely; but it seems unable to stand in either way. Not universally, that is, of all men; for before the coming of Christ many of the more ancient had greater knowledge of the mysteries of faith than many who came later and were closer to Christ —
for example, Moses surpassed those who came after him in the old law, as St. Thomas himself holds in the said article 6, and as can be gathered from Exodus 6. Likewise David surpassed the later kings, and Isaiah the later Prophets, and so with others. But after the coming of Christ there were many in the Church who came later in time and were nonetheless more learned in the wisdom of faith, as experience also shows; indeed the whole Church seems to grow from day to day in greater explication of faith. If however that rule is understood indefinitely, it will indeed be easier, and the sense does not seem foreign to the mind of St. Thomas; for he places the example only in John the Baptist and the Apostles, and so he seems only to have meant that some men of that age surpassed all others; yet even in this sense it is not without difficulty. First, because Adam, as the parent of the whole human race, seems to have had more explicit faith and greater wisdom than John the Baptist; indeed even concerning Abraham, Moses, David, and the like, that comparison seems at least uncertain. Second, after the coming of Christ many propositions of faith have been defined that were not previously of faith — such as that Christ had two wills, that the Blessed Virgin never sinned even venially, that justification comes about through an inherent quality, and the like; therefore the faith of the Church now seems more explicit than it was even in the primitive Church among the Apostles, since to have more explicit faith is nothing other than to extend it to more believable things. Finally, St. Thomas's argument does not seem efficacious, because Christ is a light of infinite activity, so to speak, and illuminates voluntarily, and therefore his greater or lesser action is not to be inferred from greater or lesser nearness in time, but from the order established by his divine wisdom and predestination, and thus he could by his will have ordained that at this or that time the Church would be more or less instructed in faith, whether that time was closer to or farther from the time of his Incarnation.

9. Second Rule from Gregory. — Fitness argument for the Second Rule. — The second rule, then, is that of St. Gregory, in homily 16 on Ezekiel, who says: As the world is led toward its end, so for us the access to eternal knowledge is opened more broadly; by which words he indicates that in the Church there is more explicit faith at any later time than at a preceding one, which is supported by that saying of the Wise Man: The path of the just, like a shining light,
goes forward and grows until the perfect day. Gregory also proves this by a certain induction; for Abraham had more explicit faith than those who preceded him, and Moses more perfect than Abraham, and David more than Moses, as he himself says, and proves from that Psalm 118: I have had understanding above the elders. And afterward John the Baptist surpassed all those who preceded him, and the Apostles even surpassed him, at least in the excellence of doctrine. Finally, a fitness argument can be added, because it is natural for a human being to proceed from imperfect to perfect and to advance gradually, and therefore in the elderly there is usually greater wisdom; but God accommodates grace to nature; therefore it is likely that he illuminated the world and the Church in like manner.

11. The said rules are sustained, and certain notes are made for them. — Notwithstanding these objections, the said rules, when properly explained, are true and can easily be brought into agreement. It is necessary, however, first to distinguish between the common people of the faithful and the leaders or heads of the Church, and to make the comparison proportionately.
Then this comparison must be made precisely in the knowledge of faith insofar as it depends on divine revelation and infused light, not in acquired knowledge, which can be obtained by human industry even in matters divine, faith itself being presupposed. And finally, comparisons of this sort are not to be understood as needing to be verified exactly and in all persons and times, but regularly and for the most part, or as they say "from the whole class," or by comparing state with state, or the heads of those states among themselves — all of which is drawn from St. Thomas, the said question 174, article 6, and from Cajetan, question 1, article 7.

13. Second pronouncement for the same First Rule. — It is rash to think anyone after the Apostles had more explicit faith. — Second qualification of the pronouncement. — Second, comparing the heads, it must be said that those persons closer to Christ who were the heads of the Church in each state were more illuminated in faith, speaking regularly. This is how St. Thomas explains his view, and this is also how the rule of Gregory is to be interpreted, and it is easily evident from his discussion, because Moses seems to have been more excellent in divine illuminations than those who preceded him; and St. Thomas says specifically that he surpassed them in knowledge of the divinity as regards its simplicity, which God showed him when he revealed that name: I am who I am, in accordance with that text of Exodus 6: I have made my name manifest to them. And afterward the Apostles received greater knowledge, as the arguments already made rightly prove; nor is it to be thought that anyone after them had greater knowledge of faith, nor could that be affirmed without rashness, as has also been sufficiently proven. I said "regularly," however, because in any state some exception can be conceived — for example, in the state of the law of nature perhaps Adam surpassed those who came after him, and in the state of the written law David perhaps surpassed Moses, Isaiah, and others, as has also been touched upon. Furthermore, John the Baptist can be compared with the Apostles; and regarding Elijah and Enoch, insofar as they are to come at the time of the last judgment, one can consider whether they will have equal or greater knowledge of faith; and thus in these matters nothing more certain can be affirmed.

14. Third pronouncement for both rules. — Third, it must be said specifically regarding the Church of Christ that with the passage of time it has grown in acquired wisdom concerning divine things, mediated by faith, as experience makes clear. Hence with regard to this wisdom there could also be change and variety in the Church, in which none of the said rules can have moral certainty; for in certain times closer to the coming of Christ the Church seems to have abounded with greater light and knowledge, there being in it more illustrious doctors, which afterward could diminish as those doctors passed away, and again afterward increase as others arrived — for this all depends on the order of divine providence, together with the diligence of the pastors of the Church; and this is proven by the difficulties raised, which are easily resolved from what has been said.

15. A small question. — Motivation for the negative part. — There remains only one difficulty still to be resolved, which was also already proposed and is of greater moment: namely, whether faith in the Church of Christ has grown, with regard to certain propositions to be believed as matters of faith, in a later time, which previously were not believed as matters of faith? For from what has been said the negative part seems to follow, because infused wisdom could not continue to grow extensively in this Church, otherwise later pastors of the Church could surpass the Apostles in this wisdom; likewise, in this Church there are no new revelations; therefore neither are there new objects of belief. Finally, the Scholastics cited above seem to hold this view, saying that the faith of the Church does not grow with respect to the number of objects of belief, but only with respect to their explanation; and St. Thomas, in this question 1, article 10, ad 1, says that nothing is taught by the Church that is not contained in the doctrine of the Apostles, but is explained more fully and proposed to the faithful on account of heretics; whence also Waldensis, Book 2 of the Doctrinale fidei antiquae, chapters 22 and 23, says that the Church cannot establish a new article of faith but only explain the ancient ones, which is also taught by Castro, Book 1 Against Heretics, chapter 8; and Cano, Book 2 of the Loci, chapter 7 and Book 4, chapter 3.

16. Prior part of the true resolution. — Posterior part. — But because this point touches on the matter of the power of the Pope and Council to define the truths of faith, which we will treat expressly below, Disputation 5, sections 1 and 8, I therefore say briefly that it must simply be asserted that the Church does not hand down a new faith, but always establishes and explains the ancient one; for that is why it always has recourse to Scripture and the Apostolic traditions, and the ancient Fathers also teach this, such as Vincent of Lérins, in the book Against the Profane Novelties of Words, chapters 7 and 37; Irenaeus, Book 3 Against Heresies, chapter 2; and
Jerome on Psalm 86: The Lord has told it in the scriptures of the peoples, and of those princes who were in it, where he expounds the word were to explain that those princes were the Apostles. Notwithstanding this, however, it is true that some proposition is now believed explicitly as a matter of faith, which previously was not believed explicitly by the Church, even though it was contained implicitly in the ancient doctrine; this is proven by the examples adduced above, and an excellent example is also that of baptism conferred by a heretic in the form of the Church — whether it should be repeated, or whether it is valid; for in the time of Cyprian neither was a matter of faith; and therefore, although he and Pope Stephen held contrary views, they nonetheless remained in the unity of the same faith, because Stephen defined nothing; but afterward it was handed down as a matter of faith that such baptism is not to be repeated; and many similar examples can be adduced, and without doubt this pertains to the defining power of the Church. Nor is a new revelation necessary for this, but the infallible assistance of the Holy Spirit suffices to explain and propose explicitly what was previously contained only implicitly in the revealed deposit.

17. The motivations of the negative part in no. 15 are answered. — And thus the said authors are to be explained. — For the explanation which they say the Church can make is sometimes by means of the explanation of a new proposition contained within the ancient ones. But that proposition is never a new article, because it does not pertain to the, as it were, substantial matter of faith to be believed explicitly by all — for that has always been sufficiently explained in the Creed — but it often pertains to the doctrine of faith that must be known by the doctors of the Church, according to the variety or necessity of the times.

18. One class of propositions that over time come to be believed explicitly. — Another class. — Finally, on account of what has been touched upon regarding the Apostles, we can distinguish a twofold order of propositions that over the course of time come to be believed explicitly. For some pertain, as it were, to the substance of mysteries — as in the mystery of the Incarnation, that Christ had two wills; and in the mystery of the Eucharist, that the substance of bread does not remain after consecration, and similar propositions. Of these kinds it must be believed that they were known by the Apostles not only implicitly but explicitly, because they understood the Scriptures most excellently, and all the mysteries that pertained to the tradition of faith. But there are other contingent propositions that had not yet come about in the time of the Apostles — such that this or that person is the Pope, that this is a
true Council, and similar matters. These did not need to be known explicitly by the Apostles, but only in a general way, because it was not necessary that all future things be revealed to them. And perhaps in this way on the day of Pentecost they were not explicitly taught about all the mysteries of faith with regard to their particular circumstances — such as the manner of the calling of the Gentiles and the cessation of the legal observances — as is plainly gathered from Acts 10 and 15. And thus also John, in the Apocalypse, understood many things about the future that had not been revealed to others, and perhaps many of these will not be understood certainly and explicitly until they are fulfilled. In this way, therefore, the Church can advance in knowing these matters, even with the certainty of faith, through the definition of the Church, which, by reason of the assistance of the Holy Spirit, has the force of revelation, or infallibly applies the universal revelation to a particular object.

And these remarks suffice concerning the material object. For the other matters that could be treated here — regarding propositions believed only mediately, or those handed down but not written — depend on what will be said about the formal object and about the rules of faith, and will be treated there.
